title: Pauri 37, sound: karam khandd

segments.voice: Yesterday, Saram Khand, the workshop where effort shapes the mind. Today, the fourth realm, sound first.

Songwriters know a trick. Later in a song, you bring back a line's exact shape with one word changed, and the listener's ear lights up. The same frame, a new filling: you've moved, but you're still in the same song. Yesterday's stanza gave a frame: saram khandd kee baanee roop, the language of the realm of effort is beauty. Pauri 37 opens with that same frame, changes two words, and suddenly you're somewhere new. One of the new words is an old friend, the word that hammered through Pauri 33. Listen for the echo.
screen: `THE SAME FRAME, A NEW WORD.` → `SARAM KHANDD KEE BAANEE ROOP.` → `LISTEN FOR THE ECHO.`

segments.voice: Here is the first line of Pauri 37: karam khandd kee baanee jor. Same frame: saram becomes karam; roop becomes jor. Karam: grace, generosity, kindness freely given. It came into Punjabi through Persian, and it's easy to confuse with karma, which means action and its results. Both appear in the Granth. Here the usual reading is grace, though some commentators read it as deeds. Karam khandd: the realm of grace. Kee baanee: its language, its mark. Jor: power, strength. The language of the realm of grace is power. In Pauri 33, jor hammered through every line with no beside it: no power to speak, no power to be silent, no power of our own. Here jor comes back, and there's no no. The power that wasn't ours is at home in the realm of grace. Then the second line: tithai hor na koee hor. Tithai: there. Hor: other, else. Na koee: not anyone. Hor again. There, no one else, no other at all. Hor bookends the line, the way jor boxed in the lines of Pauri 33. Say the two lines aloud and a strong, even beat comes through. Tomorrow, who lives in this realm, and what lies beyond it.
screen: `SARAM BECOMES KARAM.` · `KARAM — GRACE, NOT KARMA.` · `JOR — POWER, AND NO NO THIS TIME.` · `TITHAI HOR NA KOEE HOR.` · then, large: `KARAM KHANDD.`

segments.voice: Say the two lines aloud three times with a strong, even beat: karam khandd kee baanee jor, tithai hor na koee hor. Then say yesterday's line once, saram khandd kee baanee roop, and today's once more, and hear the echo. Sit in silence after, letting the beat fade with each breath out, resting without trying to earn anything.
Hor, other, else. It opens in the realm of grace: karam khandd kee baanee jor, its language is power, and there is no one else, no other at all.
Your line: karam khandd, the realm of grace. Saram became karam, and jor came home. Day two hundred twenty-six, done.

howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning; Pauri 37 describes the last two of the five realms, and its opening, karam khandd kee baanee jor, echoes the frame of the line before it about Saram Khand.
